title: Shared accommodation licensing and lodging house rules referred
subtitle: Committee also backed event staff contract authority and Laurentian Trail crossings, with lodging house zoning changes sent to June 24.
overview: The committee spent most of the evening on a proposed Shared Accommodation By-law and a related city-wide lodging house review. The by-law would license lodging houses and short-term rentals such as Airbnbs, and would add three staff positions and compliance software. Planning changes would allow lodging houses wherever residential uses are permitted. After hearing delegates and questioning staff, the committee referred both reports to the June 24, 2024 Council meeting so staff can answer open questions {{vote:m3}} {{vote:m4}}.

Questions staff will address include criminal record checks, whether the 20 currently licensed lodging houses can be protected from the new rules, parking, kitchens and bathrooms, limits on bedrooms in short-term rentals, and joint tenancy leases. Staff also agreed to provide yearly updates on lodging house licensing.

The committee also recommended that senior Culture and Entertainment staff be authorized to sign talent and sponsorship agreements {{vote:m1}}. It also recommended Cycling and Trails Master Plan spot fixes, including new crossings on the Laurentian Trail {{vote:m2}}. For residents, the main effect is that decisions on lodging house and short-term rental rules will wait until late June.

decisions.detail: The committee referred the proposed by-law, its fees, three new staff positions and compliance software to the June 24, 2024 Council meeting so staff can provide more information on issues raised.
The committee referred the Official Plan and zoning amendments permitting lodging houses city-wide to the June 24, 2024 Council meeting, since they are tied to the Shared Accommodation By-law.

The committee recommended that named Culture and Entertainment and downtown development staff be authorized to sign relevant legal agreements, and that the Director sign sponsorship agreements, to the City Solicitor's satisfaction.

The committee recommended implementing the 2024 spot fixes, including pedestrian crossovers at four Laurentian Trail crossings, a raised crossing at Lucerne Drive, no-stopping zones and a Uniform Traffic By-law amendment.

debate: A student association delegate supported licensing but said defining a lodging house as five or more people, excluding the owner, would leave many student renters outside the program. The delegate also asked for a fund to help tenants displaced if a licence is revoked.

A delegate representing a licensed lodging house owner objected to yearly criminal record checks, detailed floor plans, and a rule capping bedroom floor area at half of the home's gross floor area. The delegate said this could force the loss of rooms and asked that existing licensed houses be exempt. Councillors raised concern that exemptions could carry over to new owners, and one suggested ending any exemption on sale.

Housing advocates supported removing separation distances and lowering parking minimums. They warned the 50% bedroom rule could displace tenants and asked for clarity that revoking a licence is a last resort. Staff said revocation would be reserved for serious health and safety issues and that they were open to reducing or removing the 50% rule.

An Airbnb host said short-term rentals house newcomers and local residents, that guest reviews already weed out poor operators, and that licence fees and a bedroom limit would hurt small hosts. Some councillors said neighbours had raised valid concerns about problem units, while others wanted a softer approach to short-term rentals.

Councillors questioned the lack of rules on bathrooms and kitchens, since the Building Code and Fire Code do not set minimums. Others questioned a single parking space per lodging house compared with as-of-right fourplex requirements, and asked whether staffing would be enough for the estimated unlicensed houses.
